::: {#exm-nonconstructive-proof}
#### An irrational power of an irrational number

Claim: there are irrational numbers $x$ and $y$ (@def-irrational-numbers) for which $x^y$ is rational (@def-rational-numbers).

The number $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational (@thm-sqrt-two).
Consider $\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}$, and take two cases (@def-proof-by-cases).

**Case 1: $\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}$ is rational.**
Then $x = \sqrt{2}$ and $y = \sqrt{2}$ work.

**Case 2: $\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}$ is irrational.**
Then take $x = \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}$ and $y = \sqrt{2}$, both irrational, and

$$
\ba
x^y
&= \paren{\sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2}}}^{\sqrt{2}}
&& \text{(substitute } x \text{ and } y \text{)}
\\&= \sqrt{2}^{\sqrt{2} \cd \sqrt{2}}
&& \text{(a power of a power multiplies the exponents)}
\\&= \sqrt{2}^{2}
&& \text{(} \sqrt{2} \cd \sqrt{2} = 2 \text{)}
\\&= 2,
\ea
$$

which is rational, since $2 = \frac{2}{1}$.

Every number is rational or irrational, so one of the cases holds, and the claim is true.
The proof does not say which case holds, so it does not name a pair $x, y$ that works.

:::
